speechtext:
It should go to the nation. The munitions plants are all carried on for the nation, the Government would exercise a supervision over the wages, over the cost of manufacture, and the Empire and Canada would get the benefit of the saving.
Mr. MIDDLEBRCU You would have to reduce the contract price of the shell or the manufacturer would get the benefit.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Clearly so. The Government could control that. In that way yon would be working out a plan of national service. It does seem to me that this is a matter which the Government ought to take hold of. One step in reducing the cost of manufacture would be to reduce wages, and if you should find in any munitions factory a thousand men who under this Act would be liable to go to the front, but who say that they prefer to serve in the munitions factory, then, as a condition of their being exempted from going to the front, they ought to he willing to serve for the soldier's rate of pay. If they serve for a lower rate of pay it will bring down wages all around, and the country will get the benefit. The cost pf munitions is simply enormous; it is out of all reason, I am told. Wages are two or three times what they ought to be. It makes no difference to the munition manufacturer what wages he pays; he adds the increased wages to the cost of the product, and the Canadian people and the people of the Empire are-paying the bill. I heard the Other day of the case of a young lady in Toronto-and I believe it is the fashion in Toronto for young women to work in munition factories; the idea has gone abroad that they are doing patriotic work- I am told that this young lady was placed upon the waiting list and was allowed .so much a day while waiting to be employed. When the time came for her employment she received about two or three times the [DOT] wages received by a soldier who has gone to the front. That is only an illustration of the large wages which are paid in these factories; unskilled workmen are getting three or four times as much as the boy gets who goes to the front and risks his life in the service of his country.
I would suggest these two amendments, one as to the hearings of all these tribunals being open to the public, and that hearings shall take place only after due public notice has been given; and the other that there should be a condition attached to the exempting of a man from military service, that condition being that he might be

placed in such service as the Government might desire to place him in in the national interest; that his compensation should be fixed by officials of the Government, and that in fixing that compensation due regard should be had to the compensation which the man would receive if he had responded to the call of his country and gone to the front instead of remaining here engaging in other work.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I am pretty well in agreement with the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) as to the wisdom in general of having all the tribunals open to the public. As these tribunals are in the nature of law courts, they should be, as law courts in general, open to the public. Of course, every one knows at the hearing of any case it is within the power of the judge to clear the court room and make it a non-public sitting.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: For very substantial reasons.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Yes. Consequently my present impression is that it would be better to leave the Bill as it is, because the determination as to public sittings of the tribunals is a matter of procedure and of the constitution and practice of the court. Consequently it comes within the clause as to regulations which are to be framed by the Supreme Court judge, Known as the central appeal judge. I think that the central appeal judge would be better able to frame regulations as to public or non-pub-lie hearings in particular cases than this committee. There might be cases where it would be a gross injustice to an individual that the hearing should be in public; but in the main the hearings should certainly be public, and the principles that would apply should be practically the same as apply in courts of law.
The second amendment proposed is of a most radical and extraordinary character. If adopted in principle, much more if adopted in detail, it would mean a very radical and extraordinary change indeed in the whole commercial and industrial system of the country. I should be glad if the hon. member would supply me with a copy of the amendment at six o'clock.

speechtext: Has the Solicitor General accepted the amendment proposed by the hon. member from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Rainville), that the local tribunals shall have power to exempt men of the agricultural class?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I have made a note of the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman from Chambly and Vercheres. I cannot see, for the moment, that it will change the- legal effect of the Bill in any degree. The only reason why it might be reserved is that perhaps the amendment would make the object more clear.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres would, perhaps, make it plainer, and, as it is included in the preamble, would certainly not do any harm, and would make clear the intention of the section. Therefore, I endorse his suggestion. I would not like to say that I agree with my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), in his suggestion, because I think it is unnecessary. I think the Solicitor General, following the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), could very well take the opportunity, either in this Bill or in a concurrent Bill, to organize labour. Since the war started, we have wanted nothing greater than the organization of labour. We require that just as badly as we require an increase of taxation, which would exempt nobody, and would furnish more towards the expenses of the war as we go along. I hope the Minister of Finance is preparing a Bill, which he will introduce by the time this Bill is passed, which will impose a general and heavier taxation on the people, so that the people may pay a greater proportion of the expenses of the war, and so that less may be borrowed. There certainly will be a limit to our borrowing capacity before long, and it is not fair to the country that we should postpone until after the war, making provision for the enormous expenses of this.war. The country is more or less prosperous at the present time, and can well afford to pay more taxes. I do not refer to any special class, but I think that the people should in future pay more towards this war than they have in the past. With reference to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman from St. John, that the wages of the men throughout the country should be set on the same basis as the present pay to the soldiers, I am sorry to .say I cannot agree with him.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I did not limit it to the present pay of the soldiers.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That would create chaos in 'the labour (industry |of ;the country, which would be a very bad thing, and, furthermore, the mem could not live on the wages now being paid to the soldiers at the front; but I very strongly recommend that, either in this Bill or by some other means, the pay of the men going to the front should be materially increased. I see no reason on earth why this should not be done, and I am quite sure that it is not in proportion to the pay of other classes throughout the length and breadth of the country. If there is any one class in the world, at the present time, that should be well paid, it is the men who go to the front. It is not necessary for them to have more money while they are actually on the fighting line, buit the money could be saved for them so as to give them a start in life after they return. Now is the time to arrange that. We should not postpone it. I think the Government should take that into consideration at once, whether in connection with this Bill or not, I am not going to say, but provision should be made that the men who go to the fighting line should be more adequately compensated.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is that required by law?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it is.

speechtext: No, it is voluntary.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
They are all doing it, anyway. They are getting the combined strength of the men and women of the United States, for the purpose of this war. That makes it evident that there should be another measure put through the House almost conjointly with this one, in reference to food control, which, though perhaps not just as essential, is only secondary in importance to this measure. The women take a very important part, as the food controller has ascertained and recognized. With a Bill to provide for the registration of all other powers, as well as this manpower Bill, we would be in a position to know, at every step, what we were doing.
The reason for that assertion of mine has been made evident here today by the remarks of the members for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Rainville), St. John (Mr. Pugsley), North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). In fact, all the speakers referred to the necessity of having men spared for agricultural purposes. If we had a full inventory of our powers we would know just what we had to start with. At present no one knows what raw material we have to work on, even in respect to this Bill. It is true that we have information based on some old census returns, hut we have no definite figures as to what our raw material is in the way of man-power.
The necessity for the Bill, which, as I have suggested, should be passed concurrently with this one, has also been made evident to-day. The man who cannot go to the front ought to do something else, and that something else ought to be found for him, or pointed out to him by statute. It will be idle for us to say to one man: you must go to the front, and then excuse another man and let him go home if there be some other place in which he can do better work. The ordinary principle of compulsory service could not, to my mind, be worked out in respect to farm labour. You can compel men to do almost anything within reason when they are under military control and gathered together in numbers under the authority of officers, but you cannot compel one or two men on a farm to do this

or to do that. You have to have some arrangement under which men would be willing to go on the farms. Some provision should be made for the distribution among the different industries of Canada-a provision which I do not find in this Bill-of the men who cannot go to the front. Many men who are physically unfit for military service are fit for some other form of service. We are taking no steps to place these men in a position to relieve men who are fit to go to the front, or to provide for a distribution of the man-power that is not called upon for military service. Such distribution should take place among various industries of Canada, which will be very much crippled if that course be not adopted. The member for St. John 'suggested that the men who cannot go to the front should be asked to serve in some other capacity at the same wage as that paid to the soldiers. Theoretically, that sounds all right, but I fear that it would not work out in practice. In order to ensure the success of this measure and of the Bill that I suggest should be passed concurrently with it, steps should first be taken to secure the co-operation and sympathy of organized labour. I fear that the step suggested by the member for St. John would make that an impossibility. I suppose that if his suggestion were adopted, we would have to have a Patriotic Fund, separation allowance, pension fund, or something equivalent to all these, for the men who did not go to the front and who engaged in other work at the same wage as that paid to the soldiers. Then, to place a man in an industrial establishment at, say, $2.50 a day when a man beside him would be earning $4 or $5, would so disarrange labour that the plan could not be successfully worked out. I am afraid that the carrying out of this proposal would not secure to the Government or to Parliament that cooperation of labour organization without which none of these Bill will be very successful. It is reasonable, though, to say that every man who does not go to the front ought to be asked to do something else for which he is fitted. I again say that the Government ought to place before the House with all possible speed proposals for the co-ordination and utilization of all forces not dealt with by this Bill, because this Bill cannot be as intelligently discussed by itself as it could be if we had a measure of the kind that I have suggested to discuss with it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I realized when I moved the amendment that certain difficulties
would attend the proper working out of the proposal. But it is not impossible to devise an amendment to this Bill which would tend to equalize , the wages paid to those who engage in some other branch of the national service and the wages paid to those who enter upon active service and go to the front. I quite agree with the member for North Oxford that it would not do to fix the wages of those who engage in some branch of the national service other than military service at what is now paid to the soldiers. The reason is that this country has treated its soldiers in a most shameful manner. Canada is not paying her soldiers that to which they are fairly entitled; everybody admits that. Some gentlemen answer by saying that the soldier does not go to the front with the idea of getting adequate wages. Pushing that argument to the extreme limit, you would say that the soldiers should not be paid anything.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
What sum would the
hon. gentleman suggest that we pay the soldier and the mechanic?

speechtext: young men are to-day deterred from enlisting, 'because if they remain at home they can get $4 or $5 a day and support their families in comfort, while if they go to the front they would get only one-third of what they could get at home.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman fix the same price of $3 a day for those who are exempted, to do farm work?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why not? That would be a matter for the officials to determine who would be employed by the Governor in Council. There would be many cases, of course, of young men working at home on their fathers' farms, and receiving no wages, for ordinarily the young man on his father's farm is not paid wages. But these are exceptional circumstances which could not very well be provided for. I do not submit this amendment as being perfect. It merely suggests the principle that should be applied in the case of those who ask for exemption. If that were done I think the applications for exemption would be very much fewer than would otherwise be the case. If the man applying for exemption knows that he would not receive any more compensation in any other branch of national service than he would receive if he went to the front, he would be very much more likely to go to the front.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: My hon. friend would fix the pay of a private at $3 a day?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What rate would he fix for lieutenants and captains?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It would be very easy to determine the relative increase that - officers should receive. Those who have to do with the matter would necessarily fix the compensation. My idea in making this suggestion is to reduce the wages of those engaged in the manufacture of munitions to the rate which the soldier ought to get, or to raise the pay of the soldier to something approaching, if not equal to, the wages paid to those who remain at home. Whether that could be worked out or not I do not know. I shall, of course, be guided by the judgment of others, but it seems to me it could be worked out in a very large measure. I have another objection to this section. Paragraph (a) of subsection I, section 11, provides:
That It is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged.

Paragraph (to) provides:
That it is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he wishes to be engaged and for which he has special qualifications.
As I understand the section, once an exemption is granted under paragraph (a) or
(b)	that is the end. of the matter. It is not a conditional exemption.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Certain exemptions
must toe conditional, and any exemption may be conditional.	[DOT]

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Under what clause?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of section 11, which says:
(a) A certificate may be conditional as to time or otherwise, and if granted solely on conscientious grounds shall state that such exemption is from combatant service only.
So, any certificate may be conditional, and certain certificates must be conditional.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is expressly provided by paragraph (c) that it shall not be conditional upon his remaining in. the employment in respect of which he is granted exemption. He is not obliged, however, to remain in that establishment or in that place. If he moves, he could be called up again and could again apply for exemption.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The certificate might be conditional on his remaining at a certain class of useful work, without specifying any place or establishment.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Paragraph (to) provides:
A certificate granted on the ground of the continuance of education or training or on the ground of exceptional financial or business obligations or domestic position, shall be a conditional certificate only.
Paragraph (c) provides:
No certificate shall be conditional upon a person to whom it is granted continuing or entering into employment under any specified employer or in any specified place or establishment.
Under that, the labourer could go from place to place, leaving the employment in respect of which he had been granted exemption and engaging in some other work, and it might be very difficult to trace him.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It might be embodied in the certificate that he should report.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That might be. I just wish to say one word with regard to the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Chamrly and Vereherea (Mr. Rain-

vilJe). As I understand it, he proposes that subsection (r. be amended by inserting between the words "in" and "other" the following:	"agricultural, Industrial
or." I think the Solicitor General will agree with me that that would rather limit the exemption which would be provided for. Where specific words are used just before the word "other," the courts are guided by those specific words. In this case "other work" would mean employment of a like character to that already specified. It seems to me that that would embarrass the tribunal very much, because it would be an indication of the opinion of Parliament that no exemption should be granted except to persons engaged in agricultural or industrial work c r work of a like character. Now there might be many employments which would be just as important in the national interest, but which would be entirely separate and distinct from agricultural or industrial work. Unless the banks, for instance, have a sufficient number of employees to carry on the work of banking, it would be very difficult to carry on industrial work. Without banking facilities the business of great manufacturing establishments could not be carried on, and so also with regard to agricultural production-potatoes, cattle, wheat, flour, and everything of that kind. Without brokers to handle the business connected with the proper carrying on of that class of work the business of the country might be enormously hampered, and the work of those who are engaged in production might be very seriously interfered with. Take the question of transportation. What advantage would it be to have industrial or agricultural products unless we had transportation facilities to carry those products to the markets of the world? For these reasons I rather think it undesirable to limit the subsection by the amendment proposed by my hon. friend. I have not given the matter very much consideration, but I think upon the whole it would be very much better to leave the paragraph as it is, and it would be for the tribunal to say whether the agricultural, industrial, banking, mercantile or transportation work in which the applicant was engaged was in the national interest, and whether the applicant should be granted exemption or not.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The alleged inadequacy of the payment of our soldiers has been referred to so frequently in this
House that I think it ought to be thoroughly understood just what our soldiers receive. Take, for instance, the case of a married man with a family of two children who has enlisted in the province of New Brunswick. What is the total remuneration received by him and his family on account of his services overseas? In the first place, he gets $1.10 a day, which is $33 a month. His wife gets a separation allowance of $20 more. From the Patriotic Fund in New Brunswick she gets an average of $15 more.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: But the Patriotic Fund is .purely voluntary, and should not be counted in what the men are supposed to get.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That makes $68. The man's food is estimated at 60 cents a day, for 31 days a month, Which makes $18.60 more. His clothes, boots, cap, overcoat .and everything he requires vihile he is in service are furnished him, representing at least $10 a month more. Consequently, that man and his family receive directly and indirectly on account of the services he renders his country no less than $96.60 a month, which will figure out $3.10 a day. This is what the people of Canada as a whole pay the married soldier from New Brunswick who has a wife and two children. This is not inadequate by .any means.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Wages are not over-high in New Brunswick. They are supposed to be fair. Take the ordinary 'chauffeur for instance, who has no. family. He gets an average of from $15 to $20 per week, which is higher wages than the boy who goes to the front and risks his life.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is $20 a week paid all the year around?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, all the year round. They do not get less than $15 a week, .and many of them get $18 or $20 a week.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I may say we have not much snow in the southern part of New Brunswick, and they run the automobiles all the year round.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Mostly wind,

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, we are favoured in that way too.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In this case it is $3.12 a day, seven days in .the week, which is an average of about $22 a week.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I have made the calculation as to what the soldier gets, a little differently from my hon. friend's calculations. I quite agree he gets $1.10 a day, which is $1 a day as pay and 10 cents a day field allowance. He gets his clothing and his food which we might put at another dollar, which is the outside. He also gets his separation allowance, if he is married. If he is not married he does not get any separation allowance. The Patriotic Fund should not be counted in it, because that is a purely voluntary contribution by the people, and it should not be necessary for a country like this kind, considering the financial condition of the people to count that as part of the soldier's pay. The people should not be called upon for voluntary subscriptions to the Patriotic Fund; the Government should pay that in the form of extra pay to the men. It is more or less of a charity, though it does come voluntarily, and it is remarkably well administered. I have nothing to say against .my hon. friend from Montreal St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) on that score, because he deserves great credit for the way in which this fund has been administered. At the same time that does not affect the principle. I hold the principle is wrong, and the Government should pay the men entirely. They should pay the men more than they do, and when it comes to the married men the separation allowance should be at least $30 in place of the $20 a month, to make up for the Patriotic Fund. The separation allowance does not take a man's children into account at all. They pay the same to the married man, whether he has children or not. If you limit it to $20 a month foT the mabried man, if he has children he should 'be paid in addition, in proportion to the number of children he has. That is for the separation allowance only. The pay of the ordinary man should be increased to $1.50 a day plus the 10 cents field allowance, at the lowest calculation, and estimating his board and clothing as being worth, say, $1 a day, that would put him on the same basis as other men throughout the length and breadth of the land.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for St. .Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) is not quite fair in his statement of the case. He takes an exceptional case to prove the rule. The general rule is the men at the front are unmarried. We are proposing to send men to the front by compulsion and the plan of the Government will be that only unmarried men shall go, as far as pos-

sible. Why my hon. friend takes this exceptional case as a basis for a general conclusion I eannoit understand, if he intends to be fair, and I must assume he does intend to be fair. More than that, why should the man who is unmarried, and who is being sent to the front, receive less than the ordinary labourer at home receives? Is it a good reason to say that some other man at the front gets more than he does? I think the committee will have to acknowledge there is no justification in the world for paying men at the front less than ordinary labourers get at home.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know what men are being paid at home?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would not undertake to say, because I am not familiar with wages all over the country. If I were to talk of the wages I pay farm labourers at home, I could tell you very quickly. I pay $55 a month in summer and $30 a month in winter.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is it possible to estimate in dollars and cents the value of the services our men are rendering at the front?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is no use ringing that in. Every one knows it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is no reason not to pay a man because he is serving his country. I do not think it is fair that a man who is risking his life every day in the service of his country should receive less than an unskilled labourer at home. There is a great deal we never can pay him for.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) let me ask him a question? What is the rate of pay of a British soldier, for instance?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I wish to call the attention of the hon. member for St. Antoine to the fact that in a recent bulletin of the Patriotic Fund the statement was made that although there were 105,000 families dependents of soldiers, only 60,000 received aid from the Patriotic Fund.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: May I repeat my question to the hon. member for Frontenac, who does not wish to appreciate the real value of the services rendered by the soldiers in the trenches? How much pay does the British soldier get?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I understand the British soldier gets less than half what is paid to the Canadian soldier, and I understand the

French soldier gets a matter of a few cents a day. I think there has been more talk in this House this afternoon about the pay of the soldiers than there has been by all the soldiers over in France. There has been more kicking here about their pay than there has been by all the soldiers overseas. We all realize we cannot value the services of our soldiers in dollars and cents. How then are you going to set a figure on their pay unless you try to deal fairly with them and compare this country with other countries?
, Everybody is disposed to do the best he can for our soldiers at the front. There is no difference of opinion in regard to that on the part of the members of this House or in the country. It is all right now to get up and say that the soldier does not get enough hay. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) suggests $3 a day for a private. I doubt very much if he will find many members to agree with him. Another saye $1.50 would be about right; somebody else would get up and say $1.55, I suppose, and somebody else $1.60. The question of pay is not what has kept men from enlisting. The reason why men have not enlisted in greater numbers is that they have been encouraged to remain at home and they feel that they are justified in remaining at home. Look at the Militia Gazette and you will find that in the fall of 1914 a great many young men were gazetted as lieutenants. They got the title of lieutenant and they are still remaining in Canada. They find it more profitable to run automobile garages than to go overseas. I do not know why they took out their commissions. Others find it advisable to scoot over to the other side of the line and go to college there. It was not a question of dollars and cents or of pay with them. They did not go overseas because they thought it was safer to be here.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend tries to
make it out a virtue on the part of these young men that they are not fighting for dollars and cents. We all know that there is no money which can recompense men who go out and risk their lives. But that is no reason why we should not pay these men a fair wage. The question has nothing to do with what Great Britain or France pay their men. We are entitled to pay our men a fair day's wage for the time they put in just as well as we are entitled to pay men fairly whom we employ in ordinary labour. We have to pay a man employed in an ordinary occupation more than we
pay a man at the front. We know that the men at the front are not complaining at all. They did not join for the purpose of being paid a certain amount and we give them credit for that, but that is no reason why we should not see that they are properly paid.
Mr. MoCOIG:	I agree with my hon.
friend from North Oxford as far as the pay proposition is concerned. The average single man who is working upon a farm in Ontario is receiving in the neighbourhood of,$500 or $600 a year and his board, The argument is presented that in a great many *cases he is only employed for a few months in the year, but in most cases the average farmer employs a man all the year round. If he employs a man for only six months he will have to pay him at a higher rate than $1.10 a day. The average man employed on the farm gets $2.50 a day and you can scarcely get them at that wage. During the remainder of the time these men are employed in the industries in the towns and cities. If we are going to compel men to go to the front we should not pay them less than we ought to pay them and we should not hesitate over a few cents per day. We should pay them the rate that we should be willing to accept ourselves if we were going and I do not think there is any one here who would be willing to go to the front for $1.10 a day. I feel satisfied that the Prime Minister will look at it in that way. If we conscript men and compel them to go, we should see that they are fairly paid for their services. We are proud to see them go, they are going to defend us and I venture to say that tnere are not many of us here who are very anxious to go.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think the argument is any stronger in favour of the men who will have to respond to this law than it will be in favour of men who went under voluntary enlistment?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think there is any question that a man should be properly paid when it comes down to taking him away from an industry or employment in which he'is getting $2.50 or $3 a day, and telling him that he has to go to the front to defend us. Shall we send men to the front to defend us for $1.10 a day while we continue to prosper, make money and increase our bank accounts?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that a conscripted man should be paid more than a volunteer?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I feel that we would be justified in increasing the pay of the men who have already gone to the front. They entered at a time when the cost of living was only half what they are required to pay for the maintenance of their families throughout this country now. Their families suffered last winter and there was nobody who was called upon for assistance more than the hon. gentleman (Sir Herbert Ames) was during that time. There is no reason why we should not deal fairly and generously with those men. With reference to the exemption of men employed in essential industries and in agriculture, I would be inclined to support the amendment which is before the committee unless we get some assurance from the Prime Minister that it is the intention of the Government to make these exemptions. If the Prime Minister will give us an assurance that the men in these important industries will be exempted I would be glad to take his promise, or obligation, in the matter and I would not be so anxious to vote for the amendment. At this particular season of the year, when the farmers are being called upon for increased production, they are hesitating as to whether they can continue to increase production to the extent that is required under the circumstances because they do not know whether they will have their sons to assist them in taking off another crop or whether they will be present to put another crop in. Some crops were not put in on account of the unfavourable spring and now they cannot get help. The same difficulty will be experienced when it comes time to take off the crops. Root crops have to be cultivated, hay has to be harvested and if, on account of the backward spring they did not get the crops in earlier, it means that they should have double the help that they have upon the farms. Men will be required for putting in the fall wheat and making preparations for the next season and under those circumstances it is important that the farmer should know whether this Government, or this Parliament, is going to exempt such producers or whether we are going to conscript them the same as men from other professions and occupations. The same argument would apply to all the industries which are essential to the carrying on of the war.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. McCoig) must not be under the impression that I am asking that the farmers of the country should be exempt. I know that in the province of Quebec we have farmers

who do not deserve to be exempt because they do not produce the necessities of life. Their staying on the farm is of no service at all, but on the other hand the continuance of others on the farm is very necessary in the interests of the state.
My object in pointing that out was to emphasize the desirability of setting forth what kinds of work Parliament considered might be of more importance in particular cases even than military service. That is why the amendment was moved. It is not a question of protecting the farmer in himself, but of protecting the agricultural industry or other industries which are of vital importance to our country.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I believe that the general consensus of opinion among those already at the front is, not that the pay is insufficient at present, but that the scale of pensions should be made more adequate than it is at present. Any complaints I have heard at the front or in England have been along these lines. Our men are not complaining of the pay they receive. The French soldier receives five cents a day, the English soldier a shilling a day, less any allowance he may make to his relatives. The Canadian soldier gets in France approximately twenty cents a day for spending money, the balance being retained until he returns to England. It might be advisable to make the daily allowance in France elastic so that, particularly during the winter, the soldier could receive instead of thirty-five francs a month, fifty or sixty francs a month. But there is a strong feeling, especially during this time of high prices, that there should be a very material increase in the pensions, not only to the relatives of deceased soldiers but to soldiers who have been disabled.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I would direct the attention of the Solicitor General to clause (d) of II which reads:
That serious hardship would ensue, if the man were placed on active service, owing to
his exceptional financiall or business obligations or domestic position.
It would be better if that clause ended at "obligations" and a new clause were framed to deal with cases where domestic circumstances offer fair ground for an exemption. It might be better to say, ''financial, business, or domestic obligations." Or it might be preferable to follow the New Zealand Act in that respect and insert a new clause. Section 18, subsection

(b) of the New Zealand Military Service Act reads:	.
By reason of his domestic circumstances, or for any other reason his calling-up for military service will be a cause of undue hardship for himself or others.
That perhaps better expresses the idea sought' to be accomplished by Our clause (d). It is difficult to state exemptions in the Bill, and possibly the very best has been done by expressing in general terms the grounds of exemption. There might perhaps be one specific exemption, that which is contained in the 9 p.m. Militia Act; the only son of a widow, being her only support, is exempted from service. Doubtless in such cases the sole remaining son of a widow would be exempted under the Bill as it now appears. Subsection 3 of section 18 of the New Zealand Military Service Act deals with that point, and also with the point raised by Senator Power in the other Chamber, who introduced a Bill making special provision for the exemption of a son where a brother had been killed in overseas service. The New Zealand Act reads:
In the absence of regulations to the contrary, it shall he sufficient evidence of undue hardship on an appeal on any of the grounds specified in paragraph (d) of subsection 1 hereof, that the appellant is the sole surviving son of his parents who is of military age, and that at least one of his brothers has served in some portion of His Majesty's forces in connection with the present war and has lost his life by reason of such service.
Subclause (e) of section 11 states that exemption may be granted on account of ill-health or infirmity. This exemption will^ have to be established by medical evidence. This will be one ground of exemption which will be availed of very frequently by a great many who are liable to service under this Act. It will be very essential to eliminate any suggestion of partiality on the part of medical officers appointed by the tribunal. Has the Solicitor General in mind any safeguards which can be thrown around the administration of this section so as to prevent any suspicion of partiality in its administration by medical officers? I observed in the press a few days ago a regulation by the Government of the United States upon this very point.
I think it was to the effect that where an exemption was granted by a medical officer a second examination, or report, was required from another medical officer, and that an exemption was not conclusive or final until there had been a second report
and examination by another and independent medical officer. Will the Solicitor General inform the committee whether he has given any special consideration to this clause, and whether he has any safeguards in mind which would assist in the fair administration of this particular part of section 11?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Referring to the latter suggestion first, as to paragraph (e), subsection 1, ill health or infirmity, it must be remembered that the militia authorities, subsequent to the determination of the tribunal, will themselves medically examine every man who reports. This clause existed under the English Military Service Act, and the local Government Board published certain principles, or, perhaps, better termed explanatory notes, as to the application of this clause by the tribunals, and they called attention to that fact in particular-that, inasmuch as the man, after he passed their survey, had to undergo examination before the military officer, their duty was only to exempt under this clause such men as manifestly were, for the time being, incapable of military service. Wherever it was a case of doubt it would certainly be passed on, and left to the disposition of the medical military authorities. They say further that, in the operation of this clause, it was wise that a certificate of exemption should, in the first instance, at all events, in this case, be only a conditional certificate. In that way, they say, the clause is not abused. All that I desire to impress is that it is not likely that there will be any medical officer directly under the tribunal, or in the service of the tribunal. They will deal only, for example, with cases on medical certificate, or, perhaps, two medical certificates, where it is shown the man is incapable of appearing before them, and in cases where he is not incapable of appearing, and does appear, but is so crippled or infirm that it would be a mere formality to pass him on to the military officer.
Mr. MAROlL: I think in any case where the health of the man called upon is in doubt, the family physician, who is familiar with the family antecedents, should not be overlooked, because in the enlistments for overseas many were enlisted-I do not care to say how many-who should never have been enlisted, who are now in sanatoria and military hospitals all over the country, and are a charge on Canada. They were sent back, because they were never physically able to stand the strain. In a case of that kind, I think that, in every case where



there is a family physician familiar 'with the man's condition or antecedents, where perhaps .there was a tendency to tuberculosis or something of that kind, there should he a provision that that physician should he consulted before any decision is come to.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would urge that the previous suggestion of the hon. gentleman. from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) be taken into serious consideration by the Government, and that paragraph (b) subsection 2 be divided into two paragraphs. The first part of the clause, down to the word "obligation," refers manifestly to the individual man, the hardship is upon himself, and it is a business hardship, but in the matter of domestic relationship, the hardship is not upon the man who enlists, but upon those he leaves 'behind, and there should be a clause providing that, in case of hardship to others who are the natural dependents of the man, the question of exemption should be considered, I have in mind the case of an only son of a widow, *where, the widow was wholly dependent upon the son for support. Under this Bill it might be quite possible that that only son would be compelled to serve. Again, cases where all the sons have gone to the front but one, and the family is dependent upon the boy left at -home,

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Or partially dependent.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Or mainly dependent. It is not a hardship upon the boy in that case, but upon the family; consequently, I think, there should be a separate clause dealing with domestic relationships, and making it clear that the hardship upon other people created by the boy being taken away is that which should be considered. '	.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think the clause is
better taken altogether. It is a question entirely of obligation. The idea of the clause is obligation to others. I rather think my hon. friend from St. Antoine is not quite right in saying that if a man is under heavy business obligations, such obligations as can be performed only by himself, and those obligations are neglected, that that man alone has to suffer. I am afraid others' would suffer too. In other words, the class of people who would suffer is just as wide as the class who would suffer by reason of a man being taken from his domestic obligations. I see no reason for separating the two.
Dealing with the case of the only son of a widowed mother, who is her sole sup-

port, no one could 'be more sympathetic in regard to exempting such a man than myself. But the difficulty is that, if we start these specific exceptions we destroy the principle and spirit of our Act, and I do not know where we should end. I think we should get into an endless maze. To carry my hon, friend's point a little further, what is the difference between the only son of a widowed mother, who is her sole support, and one of three sons of a widowed mother, if the other two are perhaps at the other end of the earth where they cannot be found; or one of four sons, if the other three are crooked; or one of four sons if the other three feel no domestic obligations whatsoever, and are perhaps in some other country? I have followed out that idea to show that there is no reason for stopping where the hon. gentleman suggests we should stop, if we start specifying these exceptions. One could logically proceed till he would 'be in. an endless maze, if he started to make exceptions. I think the better plan is to lay down general principles, and leave the application entirely to the tribunal. In fact, I do not see any other practical plan.

speechtext:
The clause that we are now considering, which deals with exemptions, is one to which we should give a good deal of attention. It has been stated by the Solicitor General that the tribunals will exercise a certain amount of discretion in this matter. The clause gives the tribunals the right to exempt almost anybody. The words "domestic position" have a very wide application. I had a conversation with one of the officers acting on a tribunal of this kind in the United States, and I asked him a question on this very point. He said that the United States tribunals have no authority to grant any exemption; all they can do is recom-

mend to higher authority the cases for exemption; the higher authority then has to pass upon them. According to this clause the tribunal has a perfect right to grant exemptions and the grounds set out are &0 very wide that a tribunal, if it were so minded, could grant exemption to almost any one. The old Militia Act exempts the only son upon whom a widow is dependent. I think that is a provision that should be put in this Act; the only son of a widow should be specially exempted, just as clergymen are. This provision has been in the Militia Act from time immemorial; in all countries where there is conscription a similar provision is made.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why exempt the clergy?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The clergy are not exempt in France, but they are in other countries. They have been exempt in all our Militia Acts during the last couple of hundred years. The clergy and the only sons of widows have been exempted. I think the committee would do well to introduce an amendment to this clause to the effect that the tribunals in the first instance should do nothing more than recommend the exemption to a higher tribunal or court of appeal. That does away with the question of whether or not a man shall be exempt though what we call the legal moral risk. As a commanding officer at Valcartier I had applications from sisters, cousins, aunts and sweethearts of soldiers for the exemption of men in whom they were interested upon grounds of domestic position, business obligations, and that sort of thing. To my mind, this clause is too wide1 in its provisions. I would suggest that the Solicitor General narrow it down a little bit more, because it is a dangerous clause.
All over the country people are saying that there are clauses in this Bill under which the rich will be exempted, or at least favoured. If one member of a local tribunal happens to have, a cousin or some other relative brought before him the chances are that he will exempt that man. Further than that, a tribunal in one county may be very lax, and the tribunal in the next county very firm, and I see nothing in the Bill to prevent a young man from appearing before the lax tribunal even though it is not in his -county.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is "provided against in the Bill.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think the clause as to exemptions should be made absolutely
fMr. Currie.]
clear. Ill health or infirmity is given in the Bill as one ground for granting exemption. A man might be infirm for a few weeks with a bad cold, and he could claim exemption on that ground, though in two weeks he would be quite all right again. Or a certificate from a doctor would give him an "infirmity" at once. My experience teaches me that men can develop various forms of infirmity when they do not want to go into the trenches, and I think that will be the case here. In certain cases a certificate of exemption should only be conditional. A man suffering from varicose veins, for instance, after three weeks in a hospital, is just as good as any soldier in the ranks, but under this infirmity clause he could claim exemption and get off altogether. I think this clause should be given a great deal of consideration by the committee, because if many young men are exempted on the ground of ill health or infirmity we shall have to take the classes higher up, perhaps up to 40 years of age. No one who has not been in the army has any conception of the reasons that doctors will give in order to get a man off. At Valcartier every man was examined, of course, by a board of medical officers, and if a man had a cigarette eye-and one man out of every four	in	Canada	has a	cigaretteeye;	that is the	eye he blowsthe	smoke on-if	one	eye	was only
two degrees stronger than the other, and many men are born with this defect, the man was rejected. His other eye may be perfectly good, but although a soldier needs only one eye to shoot with the man is rejected, although he is just as good in other respects as any other man in the ranks. A slight limp will also disqualify a man. A man with a dropped arch is also rejected, although he may be able to drive a team just as well as a man with an arch like a Highlander. One man out of every four is rejected for defects that do not interfere in the slightest degree with his usefulness in the trenches. A great deal has been said about the age of the soldier. Now, a man of 40 or 45 may be just as strong and healthy, and able to- stand the trenches just as well as a man of 25, and sometimes better. I know lots of. men over 60 who went over with the first contingent and are in the trenches to-day, going strong, and they claim that they will kill off all the young men in the trenches before they get through. For the reason that this House should make a strong effort to prevent any fraud being perpetrated on these tribunals, I think this clause should be discussed further. I think,

also, that the Solicitor General should provide that a widow's only son who is her sole support should be exempted. That is the practice in every Christian country-in Europe at all events, although I do not believe it is the practice in New Zealand- and I would strongly urge that provision he made in the Bill granting exemption to a widow's only son who is her sole support.

speechtext: I cannot quite agree with my hon. friend in his last suggestion. Why should the only son of a widow be exempted when the five sons of another widow might be taken?

Wbhave seen by the newspapers recently that Great Britain is short in this respect, and in view of the urgent need for aeroplanes and airmen, I do not see why a man who is physically fit for the flying corps, and has the nerve and other necessary qualifications,-should not be allowed to join that wing. It seems to me we should be using our material to a disadvantage if we assigned such a man to some other branch of the service. I trust the Solicitor General will take that suggestion into his consideration, and, as T may not speak on the Bill again,

100.000	men that are required to-day, but should be wide enough to allow us to raise
200.000	or more men should they be required. While we are on the subject pf exemption, I may say certificates may be conditional as to time. specially to this power of exemption by which a man may be relegated by the certificate to another class nexit in order. Now as to this wholesale exempting; of course it is possible, and it may be found to be the case, if weak tribunals are formed in some localities by accident. That is why we have the right of appeal. During the fall of 1915 and the early part of 1916, it was brought to the attention of the Government-X should say to the attention of nearly all the members of the Government- that in certain districts in which recruiting had been brisk, vital industries such as coal mining, iron and steel, agriculture, and the munitions industry, were suffering by reason

While the hon. minister made that most moving speech in regard to the military necessities of the Allied armies, it will be observed that his mind was fixed rather upon the well-doing and well-being of his friends in the eastern industrial centres, and that the recruiting of men under the voluntary system for the filling of the needs of the front was only on all fours, in his mind, with the needs of the iron and steel, the coal mining and the munitions industry, and, he says, agriculture.

I shall be glad. The Finance Minister went on and read to the House a letter that he had addressed to "Dear Mr. Harmer," President of the Saw-yer-Massey Company, Limited, of Hamilton, Ontario. This was a letter in reply to one which he had received from this president of the Sawyer-Massey Company, and we must infer from the tenor of the letter that the Sawyer-Massey Company was one of those who had been protesting against such enlistment of men as would affect the welldoing and the well-being of their operations in Hamilton. In the course of this letter the Finance Minister said:
I am aware of the force of the arguments presented as I have canvassed them many times during the past few months. There is a point beyond which over-recruiting weak ns the strength of a nation for a long drawn-cut struggle.
He says in conclusion:
You may depend upon it we shall do what we can here to keep the nation strong and at

the same time put forth our best efforts in the field. .
We are going to keep the nation strong at home by taking care of the Sawyer-Massey Company first, and then we are going to take care of conditions in the field. The minister, after- having read this letter, says:
I had the view, during the concluding stages of voluntary recruiting, that the essential industries were being crippled to a certain extent by the enlisting of skilled mechanics, some of whom-I do not say all of whom- could have rendered better service, or as good service, in connection with the prosecution of the war, possibly, as if' they had enlisted, although I am the first to say that X admire above all the man who enlists and goes forward' to the front. Nevertheless in certain industries which are vital it is necessary, in my judgment, that a certain selection should he exercised.
We have, in this provision, the purpose of the Bill-to exercise a necessary selection in the interest of vital industries. I want to say that in my poor judgment, -when the Government of this country comes before Parliament with a proposal to conscript 100,000 men, under the pretense that they desire to procure these men for military service, they should frame their measure with that end in view, and if they want to make provision foT the protection of vital industries, that should be taken care of in another measure, not to introduce a means of, in a way, forcing labour into the employment of the so-called vital industry under the threat of military conscription. We know what our position is. We are one of the countries in this war. We know that the war must be won, or that the consequences to us will be very terrible. We know that it is our duty to win the war, and the Government, on behalf of their friends, the munition makers, come to this House and propose to put through a measure, in the name of patriotism, in the name of loyalty, in the name of our dead soldiers, the purpose of which shall he to assist the munition makers and the profiteers, who are making enough money to-day out of the blood and agony of the country, without having this Parliament legislate in addition on their behalf.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is labouring under a misconception, and I do not think he wishes to be unfair. At the time that letter was written to the Minister of Finance by the gentleman who manages the Sawyer-Massey Company, these were the facts:	Great Britain had sent to the
trenches something like 10,000 of her own

skilled workmen, whom she afterwards brought back to give them employment in the munition factories in England. I have in mind one shipbuilding industry where a great many of the most skilled men enlisted and went to England, arriving there about that time. Great Britain did not send these high class mechanics that were sent over there into the trenches, but they were conscripted into the munition plants, shipbuilding yards and machine shops. They wer-e trained and sent across the O'Cean, but were conscripted by the British munition workers. I think if there were any case where exemption should be provided, where men should not be allowed to leave the country and enlist to go to the trenches, it should be the case of those workers. They never should have been allowed to leave here. Hundreds of them left Canada ostensibly to go to the trenches, believing they were going there, and when they got to England, they found themselves taken out of the army, and placed at , work in munition factories.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Because they were needed. Britain needed skilled workmen. Skilled rivetters from the Collingwood shipbuilding yards enlisted, but were not allowed to go to the trenches; they were conscripted to build warships in Great Britain. The needs of this country in that regard are just as great as the needs of any other country. Anybody who knows anything about manufacturing in this country knows that, within the last year, the great increase in the cost of everything manufactured has been due largely to two things, namely, the high cost of labour, and the high cost of raw material. There is no' doubt about that. Nobody objects to paying the wages, but the fact remains

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Before you leave that
point, I understand you say that 10,000 of our men who enlisted for service in the trendies were conscripted.

The hon. gentleman was

They were conscripted
by the British Government and put into the shipyards. Is that the statement?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman had been listening, he would have heard what I stated. I said that Great Britain had sent to the trenches, and brought hack to England something like 10,000 skilled workmen. When Lloyd George took charge of

the Munition Department Ihe istarted to drive the munition factories, to get out guns .and shells to destroy the German power,-the only way in which it could be destroyed. The men had left the coal mines, the factories, workshops, shipbuilding yards and machine shops of England, and had gone to Prance, and 10,000 of them were brought back to England, and every man that they could find-even in our army in England-who was a skilled man, was put to work there. So that these men enlisting here, with the best intention in the world, expecting to go to fight the Germans, were not allowed to go after they got to England, but were put to work, as I have stated. What is wrong about that? They did not conscript the men to work for nothing in the factories, as they do in Germany, The munition workers in Canada get more than they do in any works in the world, much better pay than in the United States, and the cost to the Imperial Government of munitions made in Canada is a large percentage less than the cost of those munitions made in England, or in the United States. Everybody ' who knows the business knows that we are making them cheaper for the British Government than they can make them at home, with much cheaper labour.
I desire to refer to another matter. The most unfortunate thing in connection with the labour question is the poor quality of the labour left at home. If that labour had applied itself diligently to its work, nobody would have objected, but, from my experience of a number of plants that I have seen, I know that every month, when the pay roll is gone over, sixty per cent of the workmen have changed. Is that right? They are getting all the money they ask. They will only work two weeks in one shop. They get their money, jump and go to another shop. I say that is not fair to the men in the trenches. It is all right that these men should Teceive large wages, but that they should neglect the work and only work half time is a crime, when munitions are needed so badly at the front. Why should a skilled workman employed in a factory here be allowed to stay at home, and only give one-half of his time to the work? Then the complaint is made, "Oh, you are attempting to conscript these men in the factories." Is he any better than the trained workman, his comrade, who has gone overseas and is being shelled, for $1.10 a day? I cannot see that he is. I cannot see that there is any necessity to pay him any higher wages
than the other man, as a matter of honour and justice. That fact remains true. So that there is no cause of complaint.
These men are not making complaint by petition through the hon. member for Edmonton because they think they are going to be conscripted. Until such time as a , large body of them make complaint, it will not be necessary for the House to take up their case. Every workman in this country who is conscientious and anxious to work can get employment at the highest wages ever paid in Canada and under more satisfactory conditions than prevail in any other part of the world. The manufacturers of Canada, it may be said to their credit, are selling goods to the Imperial Government at ten pe>- cent iess than the price at which similar goods can be purchased in the United States. I do not see, therefore, that there is any reason for complaint.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Some of my hon. friend's remarks a few moments ago established the point that I made with regard to this legislation. He complains of the character of the labour that is now available for the gentlemen who are engaged in the manufacture of munitions, and he thinks it is right and proper that labour should be conscripted for the advantage of the munition manufacturers.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That is what I understand to be the purport of his remarks. I do not wish to enter into any controversy with my hon. friend; I only wish to state my own position. In order to meet an urgent military necessity, it is right and proper that we should conscript men under proper circumstances and by means of a proper law which has proper authority for its being passed. This law, I maintain, has not such proper authority. But the conscription of men for civil employment is another matter altogether. People who will submit gladly under fair circumstances to a measure of conscription in order to meet a military necessity will not submit to conscription for civil purposes for the profit of any citizen of the Dominion of Canada. In other words, they will not submit to be conscripted for the private profit of any man or any corporation. At any rate, that is the position that I take. While I am willing to support a fair measure of conscription, brought in under proper authority, in order to meet a military necessity, I certainly protest against the conscription of men for civil employment for private profit, such as is the purpose of subsection (b) of this Bill.

That is, before I could give a direct answer to my hon. friend's question. But I certainly would not, under existing conditions, support, or defend, or [DOT] countenance compelling that man to leave his civil employment to go into another for the private profit of another citizen, or 9, set of citizens, under the threat of military service provided in this Bill. I say that that is not a proper use to which to put the powers that are vested in this Bill. Such drastic action I do not consider at the present time well advised. But, assuming it to be well advised, if we are to conscript
100,000	men for military service, then we should prepare a Bill and enforce it for that purpose, not for the purpose of advantaging any private individual or corporation in civil employment. If the Government of this country were carrying on in its own name, for its own purposes, at its own cost and for the profit of the country, certain forms of industry intimately connected with the prosecution of the war, I could then see the reasonableness of conscripting labour for the benefit of that industry. But it is one thing to conscript labour for the benefit of the State and it is quite another thing to conscript labour for private profit. I suppose I will be corrected when I use the word "conscription" as applied to [Mr. Oliver.1
labour, but it is the purpose of this section to use the powers under this Bill for the purpose of, in effect, conscripting labour for private profit. To that I most strongly object.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: A young man who is working on a farm is to be conscripted. He says to the farmer: I want $100 a month. The farmer says: I will give you only $50. He has his choice, therefore, of taking $50 from the farmer or of being conscripted. Does the hon. gentleman think that that is a case which comes under his category of civil employment? These things will occur right along. Is that a hardship? Is that the case of a man being conscripted by a civil power for the purpose of making profit for a farmer?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I may not have caught the hon. member's statement correctly, but, as I gathered it, I would say that I think so. If we want 100,000 men and this man is subject to the draft and is fit to go overseas, he should go overseas. We should not use the threat of sending him overseas in order to drive him into the private employment of some other citizen.' That is an improper use of the power and authority that this Government is asking from Parliament.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not seem to think that Great Britain's experience of three years has any bearing upon cases of this kind. The member for North Sirncoe (Mr. Currie) has already shown that the British Government had to bring large numbers of men back from the trenches and fit them into industrial life. I cannot understand my hon. friend's reasoning when he says that because a man is exempted he is necessarily conscripted into industry. It may happen-I hope it will not-that labour will have to be conscripted and directed to industries devoted to the prosecution of the war. The United States are not so,slow to comprehend the difficulties that prevailed in England and other countries that sent thousands of their men to the trenches and afterwards had to withdraw them and employ them in industries. As evidence of the fact that the United States do not intend- to allow themselves to be led into the same mistakes as those made by the European countries, I find in this evening's Star a despatch from Washington which reads as follows:
The United States will sift out and exempt from fighting service labourers vitally needed in feeding, clothing, supplying and equipping the armies. Lest this nation make the same mistake England did at the outset, the Government will free such men and see to it that

they keep at their work. To this end, a corps of experts to-day began a list of industries essential as backstops of the armies in the field.
From official sources it is learned the list probably will name farmers as a general class, miners, men engaged in shipbuilding, munitions, workers of all classes, and every branch of industry that aids directly or indirectly in maintaining the military forces.
My hon. friend is very much concerned lest men. should he maintained m the manufacture of munitions. Why, to-day men working in munition factories are doing just as important work as the soldiers in the trenches. The United States are to be commended for the very careful preparations they aTe making to meet WiS extraordinary emergency. They have wiedom enough to profit by the mistakes of others.
I cannot understand why my hon. friend takes so much exception to the exemption of labour on the ground that it is conscripting labour into industry. Even if that were so, if the needs of the army required a greater effort from industry, it is only what has 'been done in England and France. The same thing applies to agriculture. Urgent as is the call for greater production to-day, I do not think there is any doubt that the call in 1918 will be stronger still, and if we do not encourage the farmer by helping him to get the labour necessary to work his farm how can we expect him to respond to the call for greater production? There is undoubtedly a great shortage of farm labour at the present time. I do not see why these tribunals should not be given discretion to look after the needs of agriculture and the necessary industries of the country.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend and other
members of the House have spoken to-night of the needs of agriculture, and have held out the suggestion that /under the provisions of this Bill men could be practically co/n

scripted into agriculture. My bon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) touched on this point to-nigiht and I want to emphasize what he said, that there is no such thing possible as conscripting men into agriculture, because conditions do not admit of it. To put an unwilling or inefficient man on a farm where only the owner and one or two other men a/re employed is simply adding to the burdens of the farmer and not helping him in his work. There are conditions -under which you may be able to conscript men profitably; for instance, where a large number of men are required on some work where they can be kept under supervision. But that cannot be done on
a farm, and to hold out to the farming community of this country that this or any other Government can conscript men for the service of the farmers is simply humbugging the farmers if they believe it, and I am afraid that many of those who held out the suggestion are aware that they are merely humbugging the farmers.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows very well that last year the soldiers in training were allowed furlough to assist in gathering in the crops, and I hope the Government will do the same with the volunteers and the conscripts this year. According to the present indications we are going to have a very big crop, and it will be a great pity if it is -allowed to stand in the field uncut for th-e want of labour. To-day our unemployed, men w-ho do not want to be employed at almost any price, are asking $100 a month to go on the farms, and m-any of the farmers cannot pay that price. These men are asking for the wages they would receive in the munition plants, and why should the munition plants go into competition with the farmer? I tlhink the country is in danger of losing a great harvest through the obstacles that are being placed ii. the way of what the hon. gentleman calls /the conscripting of labour to the farmers. It is .absolutely necessary that -the farms should have labourers, -and I should be willing to go as far as any one in this House in the direction of having a clause put in the Bill to the effect that the men who labour on the farm shall be exempted so long as they stay on- the farms; for it is just as necessary to have good crops as it is to produce munitions. I trust the soldiers in training this year, both volunteers and conscripts, will be ordered to go on the farms. Last year if they did not go on the farms they did not get any money. That was surely conscripting them, and nobody kicked.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the soldiers were not forced to go on the farms last year by any means. We had to make a written application for a man and guarantee to keep him a certain time and pay him a certain amount of mon-ey. The soldiers got that money in addition to their military pay, and it is no wonder a lot of them went on farms. It is preposterous for my hon. friend to say that the soldiers were forced to go on the farms.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What I said was that if they took their furlough they were forced to go on the farms.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: They were not forced to go on the farms if they took their furlough, for several of them worked in factories at Woodstock.

speechtext: They were not entitled to do so.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That makes no difference; that is what they did. My hon. friend does not know everything about everything. I heard him say something else tonight which has no particular bearing on this clause. He said that in Canada they were making munitions cheaper than in England.

speechtext: That is right.

speechtext: You think that is right? How much will you bet that it is right? You are the first human being I have heard say so, anyway.
