speechtext:
There has been a great deal of talk about assisting the farmer under this Bill. It was not the farmers who put in a protest in the fall of 1915 and the spring of 1916 against the voluntary enlistment of soldiers for overseas service: it was the heads of the munition plants. We have had evidence of that in this Hoirse within the last two days. Mr. McDougall of the Steel Company, Mr. Harmer of the Sawyer-Massey Company of Hamilton, and many others plagued the life out of the ex-Ministar of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes)
so he said in the House the other day. The Minister of Finance said only two days' ago:
During the fall of 1915 and the early part of 1916, it was brought to the attention of the Government-I should say to the attention of nearly all the members of the Government- that in certain districts in which recruiting had been brisk, vital industries such as coal mining, iron and steel, agriculture, and the munitions industry, were suffering by reason of the fact that the recruiting was not in any degree selective.	-
I will guarantee that it was not the representatives of agriculture but of these other industries who made the protests. It was "big business" in Canada that protested against voluntary enlistment in the fall of 1915 and in 1916, and as the result of their protests voluntary enlistment slackened, fell off, became insufficient.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: When?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Ever since.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: At what date did it start?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Some time in June, 1916; and it has continued ever since. Now we

have this conscription Bill brought in. The Prime Minister tells us it is exactly the same principle, so far as compulsion is concerned, as the Militia Act, but it has the selective principle instead of the balloting principle, so far as compulsion is concerned. We find that under these selective provisions every argument which has been brought up in this House since the Bill came into Committee confirms the idea that the Bill is essentially selective, and selective in the interests of the same men who demanded selective voluntary enlistment early in 1916, and who now demand selective compulsory enlistment. As I said before, I have no .objection to that if it is right and proper; if it is necessary; if it is honestly brought before the attention of Parliament and the country in. a Bill framed for the purpose. But what I do protest against is that it shall be smuggled through Parliament under the pretense of a Bill for the purpose of supporting the honour of Canada on the battle line. First things first. If we are to win the war, it must be won by fighting men; and if we are to increase our power on the battle front, let us cpme before the country honestly and say so, and make provisions for that purpose. Having done that, if it is necessary to take care of industrial conditions in. the country by compulsory service, let us make satisfactory preparations fpr that. But on such a question as this, where the lives of 100,000 men are involved, and where the honour of Canada is involved, let us not attempt to smuggle legislation through Parliament under false pretenses.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I could imagine a case very readily, and I am quite sure that those who inserted the same provision in the British Act knew that there would be practical applications of it or they would not have inserted it. The provision in the British Act is the very same as ours. I would in general terms say that if a man belongs to a class called out, and if he shows that at that time he is approaching the termination of a certain educational period, the results of which would he lost if he came just at that time, but that if he deferred for a week or two, or a month or two, that condition would be over and consequently he would be enabled to render better service to the state-that would be a class of eases that would come under that provision. I do not say that there would not he otheT classes. We had the advantage of the presence of Major Murray, who had to do with the working out of the several exemption provisions of the British Act, and we got no recommendation that this clause should be left out. We got many which we thought were useful and which we availed ourselves of. The working out of the British Act did not indicate that there was any danger in putting that clause in, hut, on the contrary, indicated that it would be useful.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say, with reference to this clause (c), that he is going to take into consideration some of the suggestions that have been made?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, I have a note of practically all the suggestions that were made.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
consider them?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, they will be given very careful consideration and the decisions will be communicated to the committee, and if thought fit a .motion can be made to return to the clause.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In regard to paragraph (c), I think the Solicitor General might have given the committee the reasons that appeal to his mind for the insertion of this provision. It hardly seems enough to say that it appeared in the British Act. There has been a large enlistment under the voluntary system from our institutions of higher education. I do not know how many hundreds, if not thousands, of young men who were taking courses in the colleges and high schools have volunteered and have formed a very valuable part of the army at the front. It seems rather strange that, that condition having existed in this country, we should make special provision for the exemption of that particular class of men.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
must remember that any exemption granted under this clause must of necessity be a conditional exemption. No absolute exemption can be given to any man under that clause. A reference to sub-paragraph (b) of sub-clause 2 makes that clear. It is manifestly made to cover the necessity for temporary exemption for the purpose of enabling a man to complete a process of education that is near completion .at the time of the call to report for duty. I should think that would constitute the great majority of cases that would come legitimately under that clause. For example, a man might be within a week of the termination of his examination foT a profession. No one would contend that it would be in the national interest that that man should report for duty until that work was done. Unless such a clause as that is in, I do not think the tribunal would be empowered to permit a man to wait until the termination of the week and then report for duty.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am quite satisfied with the propriety of the action suggested by my hon. friend, but there is another side to it. While he says it is the intention that this provision shall apply in such cases as he has mentioned, the clause does not

say so and it would be .quite possible under this section for one who was of military age to secure exemption by simply entering one of those educational institutions.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Not to secure it, because unless there was a special case an appeal would immediately overrule any tribunal which would give a man exemption just because he had entered an educational institution.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That may be so, but this circumstance might arise. If it does not mean what it says, that is different. That is what it says and I would, of course, assume that it meant what it said.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
leaves out the first phrase of the subsection "that it is expedient in the national interest." It does not make it expedient in the national interest to exempt a man who enters an institution to avoid military serviice. It is for the tribunal to determine whether it is or not and if the tribunal determines wrongly it will be corrected.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I want to say a word in regard to this matter of appeals. My hon. friend and1 I have discussed the merits of the case relating to the judgment of these tribunals and I shall not continue the discussion. When a decision has been rendered by the tribunal, if that decision is against the national interest, then the question can only be raised by the Government itself. It is under the authority and initiative of the Minister of Militia that an appeal is taken in case a decision is supposed to be adverse to- the country. Beyond any question, that leaves the matter absolutely in the hands of the Government to force an appeal, or not to force an appeal, as they please, and it leaves the matter in this shape, carrying out the suggestion- of my hon. friend from Montreal, St. James (Mr. Lapointe)-given judges who are favourable to wide exemptions, and given the sympathy of the Government in the matter, the Act becomes a dead letter in so far .as particular sections of the country are concerned. When I spoke strongly earlier in the day in regard to the propriety of demanding' a certain quota of men according to population from different sections of the country, I did it because if that provision were inserted this contingency of which I spoke could not arise, but that provision not being inserted that contingency can arise, and I am bound to believe that it is with the view of acting on that contingency that the elementary

provision requiring a quota is not included in the Bill.
On paragraph (c) subsection 5, section 11:
Notwithstanding anything in this section contained, the Governor in Council may by regulations abolish any local tribunal, and transfer its duties and powers to any other local tribunal.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the purpose of this last subsection?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It was thought that as the work proceeded it might be found that there were too many local tribunals, and that in that event provision should be made for consolidating tribunals. This is the provision. The powers of any tribunal may be transferred to another, and then the other takes the place of the first one, and may carry on anything that the first one has had under review.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is there any stipulation making it obligatory upon a man to appeal to a certain tribunal? Must he appeal where his residence is? What would prevent a man, if he should feel that one local tribunal was easier to pass than another, from going into the other district and appearing before the local tribunal where he thought his chances of securing exemption were best?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent him. A man may make his selection in his own province. If it is good enough for him, it is good enough for the department. But having made his choice, he must abide by it.	.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is it not likely to become something like the divorce law in the United States, where men go to the state where it is most easy to obtain a divorce, Nevada, for instance?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: If a man gets a divorce in Nevada, there is no appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States, but here we have a system of appeals. With the other plan the danger would be that we would have a great many questions of domicile.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 7, section 11:
When a certificate is lost, destroyed or defaced, the tribunal by whom it was granted shall, upon the application of the man to whom it was granted and upon payment of a fee of fifty cents, issue to him a duplicate of such certificate.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the purpose of levying a fee of fifty cents?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is a precaution against the certificate being too lightly lost. We had to take a more exacting precaution than this in connection with the . exodus regulations.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Who gets the fee?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is the intention that it shall go to the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. I think under the law it does not become the property, of the tribunal unless it is made its property.
On subsection 2, section 12:
(2)	All proclamations and regulations shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette and in such other manner, if any, as the Governor in Council may think necessary to ensure knowledge thereof by all persons concerned, and shall forthwith be laid before Parliament if then in session, and if not in session within ten days after the next meeting thereof.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think the proclamations should be published once in a newspaper in each county town where the boards are to sit. The Canada Gazette is not widely circulated, and comparatively few people ever get it.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is not important.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it is important enough to let the people know what is being done.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I agree that the Gazette publication really gives little or no publicity. It simply enables the newspapers to get it. The most of the proclamations are important, and they should be published in local newspapers. It may be necessary to utilize the poster system or billboards, but as to the publication of newspapers, there can be no question. The only reason that section was inserted as it is was that some minor regulations and changes might have to be made, and it would not be wise to insist on the publication because it might involve too much expense. The House may take the assurance that an important proclamation will receive wide newspaper publicity.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the peace officer appointed under this section be under military control?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, this is a civilian Bill, under a civilian minister, and the Governor in- Council appoints the peace officer and other officers to carry out the provisions of the Act. They will be in no sense military officers. They are peace officers.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I observe
that in this section there is provision to remunerate the registrars. Paragraph (a) reads:
Define the duties of registrars and fix their remuneration.
And subsection (f) says:
Make provision for expenses and the remuneration of officers.
I assume, therefore, that the members of the tribunal will not be remunerated.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The intention is that
they shall not be remunerated.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Subsection 3 reads:
All regulations shall have the same force and effect as if they formed part of this Act.
The Solicitor General said that the tribunal should be granted, in some measure, by memoranda or letters of direction. Would those directions be a part of this Act under that section-?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think that the circular, as it is called, relating to constitution, functions and procedure of local tribunals, published in Great Britain, Should be called regulations. Although they constitute general indications to the tribunals looking to uniformity, it would be impossible, and it would be barbarous drafting, to insert such provisions as are in this circular in the Act. Consequently, I am not quite certain whether it was intended that this should be among the regulations which, under the Act, should form a part of -it or not. I 'am informed they are not pant of it. But sudh as are regulations have the force of law. They must be consistent with this Act, and they -must look to the carrying out of this Act and nothing but this Act.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Lt is not contemplated
ithat such directions, or such a circular, addressed to the tribunals in operation under this Bill, will be a part of the Act?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
No, not -directions of
the nature of those I hold in my hand.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I call attention to paragraph (c), subsection 11, seo-tion 12, which reads as follows:
(c) Prescribe the conditions as to time or otherwise under which applications for certificates may be made, deferred applications received, appeals entered and heard and rehearings had, and prescribe forms.

Section 10, subsection 3, paragraph (b), reads:	.
(b) The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Central Appeal Judge may make regulations governing the right to and fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal to the Central Appeal Judge, provided any person authorized by the Minister of Militia and Defence may as of right enter and prosecute such appeal.
We have here two powers to make the same regulations. Under paragraph, (c) of section- 12, the Governor in Council is authorized to make regulations concerning appeals and re-hearings, and under section 10, subsection 3, paragraph (b), the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the appeal judge, may make regulations governing the right to appeal, and fixing the conditions of appeal. It seems to me there is a clashing, or a tautology.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The intention is that
under section 12, the Governor in Council may make regulations, as to time or otherwise, under which deferred applications may be received and appeals entered, and it is not provided that it shall be on the recommendation of the central appeal judge. That refers to the conditions under which appeals may be entered, and nothing more. On the other hand, section 10, subsection 3, paragraph (b) provides that the Governor in Council may make regulations, on the recommendation of the central appeal judge, fixing the conditions of appeal from an appeal tribunal. That is not in regard to the entering of an appeal, which is dealt with in paragraph (e), of section 12.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Would it not oau-se confusion, and would it not be better to have one provision?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
This matter was drawn to my attention yesterday by the right hon. gentleman, and I am disposed to think it might be well to take a portion of paragraph (c) of section 12, and insert it under paragraph (b), subsection 3, clause 10. I suggest that we defer consideration of this portion of section 12.
iSubsection stands.
Progress reported.
